sections.title: Section 1 — Lines 1–13 — Aeneas begins his story

intro.body:
Publius Vergilius Maro (70 to 19 BC) wrote the Aeneid in the last ten years of his life, under the emperor Augustus. It is an epic poem in twelve books about Aeneas, a Trojan prince who escapes the fall of Troy and, guided by fate and the gods, sails west to Italy, where his descendants will found Rome. Augustus claimed descent from Aeneas’ son, so the poem also celebrates Rome and its new ruler.

In Book 1 a storm drives Aeneas and his ships onto the coast of Africa, near the new city of Carthage. Its queen, Dido, welcomes them and holds a banquet in their honour. At the end of the banquet she asks Aeneas to tell his story from the beginning. Books 2 and 3 are his answer, told in his own voice.

The Greeks have besieged Troy for ten years. In Book 2 Aeneas tells how the city finally fell, not in battle but by a trick: the wooden horse.

The first passage (lines 1–56). The Greeks build the horse, hide their best warriors inside it and pretend to sail home. The Trojans pour out to look at it and argue about what to do. The priest Laocoön warns them not to trust it and hurls a spear into its side.

Between the passages (lines 57–194). Shepherds drag in a young Greek, Sinon, who tells a clever, tearful story: he says the Greeks wanted to sacrifice him, and that the horse is an offering to Minerva which will bring Troy good fortune if it is taken into the city. The Trojans believe him.

The second passage (lines 195–253). Two huge serpents come across the sea from Tenedos and kill Laocoön and his sons. The Trojans take this as punishment for his attack on the horse, break open their walls and drag it in. Cassandra warns them, but no one believes her, and the city celebrates as night falls.

The Aeneid is written in dactylic hexameter: six beats to a line, each a dactyl (long, short, short) or a spondee (long, long). The Latin here is printed with the long and short vowels marked, and the curved mark under a word’s last letter shows an elision, where that vowel runs into the next word and is not pronounced. Fast dactyls suit speed and excitement; slow spondees suit weight, effort or sadness.

  • Word position: important words placed first or last in the line, or carried over to the start of the next line (enjambment).
  • Word order: words that belong together pulled apart, or wrapped around others, for effect.
  • Sound: alliteration, assonance and onomatopoeia, especially in the serpent passage.
  • Imagery: the horse as a mountain and a pregnant belly, the bull simile, fire and night.
  • Speech: Laocoön’s urgent questions and exclamations.

1. Aeneas is telling this story to Dido. How does that affect the way he tells it?
  2. How does Virgil make the Trojans’ mistake seem understandable, even though the reader knows it is fatal?
  3. Is Laocoön a hero, a victim, or both?
  4. What part do the gods play in the fall of Troy, according to these passages?
  5. Choose the moment you find most vivid in the two passages and explain how Virgil achieves the effect.

intro.body:
Herodotus came from Halicarnassus, a Greek city on the coast of Asia Minor (modern Bodrum), and lived from about 484 to about 425 BC. His Histories, in nine books, tell how the Greeks and the Persian Empire came into conflict, building up to Xerxes’ invasion of Greece in 480–479 BC and its defeat at Salamis, Plataea and Mycale.

He says in his first sentence that he is setting out the results of his enquiry (ἱστορίη, the word that gives us ‘history’) so that the great deeds of Greeks and foreigners alike should not be forgotten. Cicero called him the father of history; other ancient critics thought him too ready to believe a good story. Both views have something in them. He travelled widely, questioned the people he met, and often reports more than one version of an event, but he also loves a remarkable tale and will break off his main narrative to tell one.

All three passages here are such breaks. Each is a complete story in a few dozen lines, and each says something about how justice works in a world where the gods take a hand in human affairs.

Herodotus wrote in Ionic, the dialect of the eastern Aegean, not the Attic of Athens that GCSE Greek is based on. The set text has been partly brought into line with Attic (θάλαττα, not Ionic θάλασσα), but some Ionic forms remain, such as ἐς for εἰς, μιν for αὐτόν and σφι for αὐτοῖς. They are explained where they occur.

How Arion was saved by a dolphin (1.24). Told while Herodotus is describing Periander of Corinth. A famous singer, sailing home rich from Italy, is robbed by the crew of his own ship and forced into the sea; a dolphin carries him to land, and back in Corinth the sailors are caught out in their lie.

The story of Euenius (9.93–94). Told during the account of the battle of Mycale in 479 BC, because the Greeks’ seer there was Euenius’ son. A guardian of sacred sheep is blinded by his fellow citizens for letting wolves kill them; the gods punish the city, and Euenius is compensated, though not in the way the citizens intended.

Respect for suppliants enforced by an oracle (1.157–159). After Cyrus of Persia conquers Lydia, the Lydian Pactyes leads a revolt, fails, and takes refuge at Cyme. The Persians demand him back, and the people of Cyme ask Apollo what to do. The god’s answer is not the one anybody expected.

As you read, think about what the three have in common: wrongdoing that is found out, people who try to manage the gods or each other, and how hard mortals find it to understand what the gods want.

Alliteration
The same sound repeated at the start of several words close together.
Antithesis
Opposed ideas set against each other, often in balanced phrases; in Greek, often marked by μέν … δέ.
Asyndeton
Clauses or words strung together with no connecting words.
Chiasmus
Words or ideas arranged in a mirror pattern, A B B A.
Delay
Holding back an important word to the end of a clause or sentence, so that it lands with weight.
Direct speech
A character’s actual words, quoted.
Dramatic irony
When the reader understands something that a character does not.
Framing
Placing two related words or ideas around others, at the start and end of a phrase or passage.
Juxtaposition
Placing two words side by side so that they react with each other, often for contrast.
Litotes
Understatement by denying the opposite: ‘not unaware’ for ‘well aware’.
Polyptoton
The same word repeated in different grammatical forms.
Polysyndeton
More connecting words than are needed (‘and … and … and’).
Promotion
Moving a word to the front of its clause for emphasis.
Superlative
The ‘most’ form of an adjective or adverb, often used for emphasis.
Tricolon
A group of three words, phrases or clauses, often building to a climax.

1. In each story someone tries to hide what they have done. How is the truth brought out, and by whom?
  2. Which character do you sympathise with most in each story, and does Herodotus seem to want you to?
  3. How do the gods show what they want in these stories, and how well do the humans understand them?
  4. Herodotus could have left all three stories out of his history. What do they add to it?
  5. Choose one moment from each story that you think Herodotus tells especially well, and explain how he does it.

sections.title: Lines 1–6 — Arion sets sail for home
sections.desc: Rich from a tour of Italy and Sicily, the cithara-player Arion sets out from Tarentum, trusting a ship of his fellow Corinthians.

sections.title: Lines 6–15 — The sailors’ plot
sections.desc: At sea the crew plot to throw Arion overboard and keep his money. Given the choice of suicide or the sea, he asks to sing one last time.

sections.title: Lines 16–23 — The last song
sections.desc: Dressed in all his finery, Arion sings from the stern and leaps into the sea; a dolphin, so they say, carries him to Taenarum.

sections.title: Lines 24–32 — Periander’s trap
sections.desc: Arion reaches Corinth, but Periander does not believe him; when the sailors arrive, he confronts them with the man they left for dead.

sections.title: Lines 33–40 — The sacred sheep
sections.desc: At Apollonia the sacred flocks of the Sun are guarded each night by the city’s leading men; it is Euenius’ turn.

sections.title: Lines 41–49 — The wolves
sections.desc: Euenius falls asleep, wolves kill sixty sheep, and he tries to hush it up. The Apollonians blind him, and at once their flocks and fields stop bearing.

sections.title: Lines 50–57 — The oracles speak
sections.desc: Dodona and Delphi reply that the gods sent the wolves, and will not stop until Euenius has whatever recompense he chooses.

sections.title: Lines 58–64 — A devious plan
sections.desc: Keeping the oracles secret, the Apollonians send men to sit with Euenius and steer the conversation round to the compensation he would want.

sections.title: Lines 65–72 — Euenius chooses
sections.desc: Not knowing of the oracle, Euenius asks for the finest farmland and the finest house in the city, and is told this is exactly what he will get.

sections.title: Lines 73–76 — The gift of prophecy
sections.desc: Euenius is furious to have been tricked, but receives what he chose, and with it the power of prophecy that made him famous.

groups.label: Respect for suppliants enforced by an oracle

sections.title: Lines 77–86 — Pactyes at Cyme
sections.desc: The Lydian Pactyes flees to Cyme and the Persian Mazares demands him back. The Cymaeans consult Apollo at Branchidae, who says: hand him over.

sections.title: Lines 87–92 — Aristodicus objects
sections.desc: The Cymaeans are ready to obey, but Aristodicus doubts the messengers’ report and goes with a second embassy to ask again.

sections.title: Lines 93–100 — Aristodicus asks again
sections.desc: At Branchidae Aristodicus puts the question himself: a suppliant fleeing death, a Persian demand, and a city that dares not act without a clear answer.

sections.title: Lines 101–105 — The sparrows
sections.desc: The god gives the same answer. Aristodicus walks round the temple, deliberately removing the sparrows and other birds nesting there.

sections.title: Lines 106–114 — The god’s reply
sections.desc: A voice from the shrine rebukes him for taking its suppliants; when Aristodicus throws the charge back, the god reveals the purpose of his answer.

intro.body:
Cornelius Nepos was born around 110 BC in Cisalpine Gaul, the Po valley in the north of Italy, and died around 24 BC. He spent most of his life in Rome as a man of letters rather than a politician, and counted Cicero and Atticus among his friends; Catullus dedicated his book of poems to him.

His best-known work, De Viris Illustribus (On Famous Men), was a collection of short lives in at least sixteen books, arranged in pairs so that Romans could be compared with foreigners: generals with generals, historians with historians. Only the book on foreign generals survives complete, together with lives of Cato the Elder and Atticus. The Life of Hannibal comes near the end of that book.

Nepos writes biography, not history. He wants his readers to understand character and to draw moral lessons, so he chooses revealing episodes, skips over long campaigns in a sentence, and often tells us directly what to think. His Latin is generally plain and clear, which makes him a good author to read early, but he can be compressed, and he likes neat contrasts, superlatives and pointed closing phrases.

<dl><dt>264–241 BC</dt><dd>The First Punic War. Hannibal’s father Hamilcar commands in Sicily; Carthage loses and must give up the island.</dd><dt>237 BC</dt><dd>Hamilcar goes to Spain to build a new empire for Carthage, taking the nine-year-old Hannibal, who swears never to be a friend of Rome.</dd><dt>221 BC</dt><dd>Hannibal, aged about 25, takes command of the Carthaginian army in Spain.</dd><dt>219–218 BC</dt><dd>He captures Saguntum, a city allied to Rome, which starts the Second Punic War, then marches over the Pyrenees and the Alps into Italy.</dd><dt>218–216 BC</dt><dd>Victories at the Ticinus, the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae, the worst defeat in Rome’s history.</dd><dt>216–203 BC</dt><dd>Years in southern Italy without the reinforcements or siege equipment to take Rome itself.</dd><dt>203–202 BC</dt><dd>Recalled to defend Carthage, he is defeated by Scipio at Zama.</dd><dt>196–195 BC</dt><dd>As suffete, one of Carthage’s two chief magistrates, he reforms the city’s finances; accused by his enemies of plotting with Antiochus, he flees.</dd><dt>195–183 BC</dt><dd>Exile: at the court of Antiochus III, briefly on Crete, then with Prusias of Bithynia. When Rome demands his surrender he takes poison, in about 183 BC.</dd></dl>

A-level questions on Nepos ask how he presents Hannibal, and how his Latin shapes the reader’s response. Things to look out for as you read:

  • the narrator stepping in to judge, compare or reassure (quod nemo dubitat, non est infitiandum);
  • comparisons between Hannibal and Rome, and between Hannibal and the Carthaginians who undermined him;
  • superlatives and sweeping words (omnes, semper, numquam);
  • antithesis and balanced clauses that sum up a judgement in a phrase;
  • speed: whole campaigns in a sentence, and slowing down for the episodes that reveal character, such as the oath, the snakes and the poison.

1. Is Nepos’ Hannibal a hero, a villain or a tragic figure? Use examples from at least three chapters.
  2. How does Nepos manage to praise Rome’s greatest enemy without offending his Roman readers?
  3. Nepos gives as much space to Hannibal’s exile as to his war in Italy. Why might a biographer make that choice?
  4. How important is cunning, as opposed to courage, in Nepos’ picture of Hannibal?
  5. How reliable do you think Nepos is? Where does he show awareness of his sources, and where does he simply tell a good story?

intro.body:
Publius Vergilius Maro (70 to 19 BC) was born near Mantua in northern Italy. After the Eclogues and the Georgics he spent the last ten years of his life on the Aeneid, an epic in twelve books on the Trojan prince Aeneas, who escapes the fall of Troy and, guided by fate and the gods, sails west to found the people from whom Rome will come. He died before he had finished revising it, and Augustus had it published against his wishes.

The poem looks back to Homer (Books 1 to 6 are an Odyssey of wandering, Books 7 to 12 an Iliad of war) and forward to Augustus, who claimed descent from Aeneas’ son Iulus. Again and again it asks what Rome’s greatness costs, and Book 4, the story of Dido, is where that cost is felt most sharply.

Dido was a princess of Tyre in Phoenicia. When her brother Pygmalion murdered her husband Sychaeus for his wealth, she fled with a band of followers to Africa and founded Carthage. She vowed to stay faithful to Sychaeus’ memory and refused all suitors, among them the African king Iarbas.

In Book 1 a storm sent by Juno, who loves Carthage and hates the Trojans, drives Aeneas’ fleet onto the African coast. Venus, his mother, makes sure that Dido welcomes him, and has Cupid kindle love for him in her heart. At a banquet Aeneas tells the story of Troy’s fall and his wanderings (Books 2 and 3).

The first passage (lines 1 to 128) shows Dido’s love taking hold and the goddesses’ plan to unite the pair. Between the passages, they come together in a cave during a storm; Rumour spreads the news; Iarbas complains to Jupiter, who sends Mercury to order Aeneas to leave; Aeneas prepares in secret, and Dido confronts him. The second passage (lines 529 to 629) covers the last night before he sails, his departure and Dido’s curse. Book 4 ends with her death on the pyre.

The Aeneid is written in dactylic hexameter, six feet to a line, each a dactyl (long, short, short) or a spondee (long, long), with the fifth foot almost always a dactyl and the sixth two syllables. Virgil uses the rhythm to shape meaning: heavy spondees for weight, grief or effort, quick dactyls for speed or excitement.

  • Word order: words separated for effect (hyperbaton), framing, emphatic first and last positions in the line.
  • Enjambment: a sentence running over into the next line, with weight falling on the first word there.
  • Sound: alliteration, assonance, elision.
  • Imagery: above all the wound and the fire of Dido’s love, which run through the whole book.
  • Speech: rhetorical questions, apostrophe, exclamation.

1. How far is Dido responsible for her own tragedy, and how far is she the victim of the gods?
  2. How does Virgil keep the reader’s sympathy with Dido, even when she is at her most furious?
  3. Trace the images of fire and wounding through the two passages. How do they change?
  4. What does the set text suggest about the cost of Aeneas’ mission to found Rome?
  5. How would an Augustan Roman reader have heard Dido’s curse at the end of the second passage?
